subject: physics

items.q: A beam of rays travelling parallel to the principal axis passes through a convex lens. What happens to the rays?
items.correct: They are refracted so that they meet at the principal focus
items.misconception: They are reflected from the lens surface to a point in front
items.why: Lenses and mirrors are met together in the same topic, both are smooth and shiny, and both produce images that can be described as real or virtual. Students transfer the mechanism they already know from mirrors onto the new object. The specification is explicit: a lens forms an image by refracting light. Light goes through a lens and is bent as it enters and as it leaves. A little light does reflect off the surfaces, but that is not how the image is formed.
items.random_wrong: They are refracted so that they meet at the focal length

items.q: What is meant by the focal length of a convex lens?
items.correct: The distance from the lens to the principal focus
items.misconception: The distance from the lens to the image it produces
items.why: In practical work the quantity students actually measure is often a lens-to-screen distance, and when a distant object is used that distance really is close to the focal length. They then generalise it to every object position. The focal length is a fixed property of the lens: the distance from the lens to the principal focus. Moving the object changes where the image forms but never changes the focal length.
items.random_wrong: The distance the object must be to give a sharp image

items.q: A lens forms an image. Where is the light changed in direction?
items.correct: It is refracted as it enters and as it leaves the lens
items.misconception: It is reflected from both surfaces of the lens
items.why: Lenses and mirrors are met together in the same topic, both are smooth and shiny, and both produce images that can be described as real or virtual. Students transfer the mechanism they already know from mirrors onto the new object. The specification is explicit: a lens forms an image by refracting light. Light goes through a lens and is bent as it enters and as it leaves. A little light does reflect off the surfaces, but that is not how the image is formed.
items.random_wrong: It is refracted only at the surface where it leaves

items.q: Which statement about the image produced by a concave lens is correct?
items.correct: It is always virtual, whatever the object distance
items.misconception: It is real when the object is beyond the principal focus
items.why: Students learn that the image from a convex lens changes as the object is moved, and assume the concave lens must behave the same way at some object distance. The word 'lens' carries the expectation of focusing. A concave lens spreads light apart at every object distance, so the refracted rays never meet and can never form an image on a screen. The specification states without exception that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.
items.random_wrong: It is real and inverted, like a convex lens image

items.q: An object is placed between a convex lens and its principal focus. What kind of image is formed?
items.correct: A virtual image, upright and larger than the object
items.misconception: A real image, inverted and larger than the object
items.why: Almost every ray diagram students draw first has the object outside the principal focus, which does give a real, inverted image. The one case that behaves differently, the magnifying glass, is rarely drawn as a ray diagram. When the object is nearer to the lens than the principal focus, the refracted rays leave the lens still spreading apart. They never meet, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified. That is exactly how a magnifying glass is used.
items.random_wrong: A virtual image, upright and smaller than the object

items.q: Which observation shows that an image formed by a lens is real rather than virtual?
items.correct: It can be formed on a screen placed where the rays meet
items.misconception: It can be seen by an eye that looks through the lens
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'virtual' is 'not actually there', which students take to mean invisible. The magnifying glass they use every day gives a virtual image that is perfectly easy to see, so the label feels wrong. Real and virtual describe where the light goes, not whether the eye can see it. For a virtual image the rays only appear to come from the image position, so no light arrives at a screen placed there — but the eye, looking through the lens, sees it clearly.
items.random_wrong: It is the same way up as the object that produced it

items.q: In a ray diagram for a convex lens, how is the ray from the top of the object to the centre of the lens drawn?
items.correct: It carries straight on without changing direction
items.misconception: It is refracted towards the principal focus
items.why: Students are taught that a lens refracts light, and apply that rule to all rays without exception. The reason the central ray is undeviated — the two surfaces are effectively parallel there, so the small sideways shift is ignored — is not obvious from the drawing. At the centre of the lens the front and back surfaces are parallel, so the ray emerges travelling in its original direction. In ray diagrams the central ray is always drawn as a straight line through the lens, and it is that straight ray which fixes the size and position of the image.
items.random_wrong: It is refracted so that it leaves parallel to the axis

items.q: In a ray diagram for a concave lens, a ray arrives parallel to the principal axis. How is it drawn after the lens?
items.correct: It diverges, as if it had come from the principal focus
items.misconception: It converges to the principal focus beyond the lens
items.why: The convex ray rule is learned first and thoroughly, and the concave diagram looks superficially the same — a line, an axis, a focus marked on each side. Students reuse the rule they know. A concave lens diverges light, so the refracted ray moves away from the axis. To find the image the diverging ray must be traced backwards, and that construction line passes through the principal focus on the object side. This is why the image is virtual.
items.random_wrong: It carries straight on, since the lens cannot focus it

items.q: A student draws ray diagrams for a convex lens and a concave lens using the same object. Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: Both refract the light, but only the convex lens converges it
items.misconception: Both refract the light, and both can produce a real image
items.why: Students learn that the image from a convex lens changes as the object is moved, and assume the concave lens must behave the same way at some object distance. The word 'lens' carries the expectation of focusing. A concave lens spreads light apart at every object distance, so the refracted rays never meet and can never form an image on a screen. The specification states without exception that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.
items.random_wrong: Only the convex lens refracts light, the concave one reflects

items.q: An object 5 mm tall produces an image 15 mm tall. What is the magnification?
items.why: Students order the two quantities in the order the story happens — object first, then image — rather than in the order the equation states. The two heights are so similar in kind that neither position feels obviously wrong. The equation is given as magnification = (image height)/(object height): the image height goes on top. Using it upside down turns every enlargement into a number below 1 and every reduction into a number above 1, which is a useful check.

items.q: An object 8.0 cm tall produces an image 2.4 cm tall. What is the magnification?
items.why: The everyday word 'magnify' means 'enlarge', so a magnification below 1 sounds self-contradictory. Students who get 0.3 assume they have inverted the equation and turn it upside down. In physics magnification is just the ratio of the two heights. Above 1 the image is enlarged, below 1 it is diminished, and exactly 1 means it is the same size. A concave lens always gives a magnification below 1.

items.q: An object 40 mm tall produces an image 8.0 cm tall. What is the magnification?
items.why: Students correctly learn that magnification has no unit, and then reason backwards that the units cannot matter at all. The cancelling only works when the two units are identical, which is easy to miss. Units cancel only when they are the same. Dividing 8.0 cm by 40 mm as though the numbers alone mattered gives 0.2 instead of the correct 2 — wrong by a factor of ten. Convert first so that both heights are in mm, or both in cm.

items.q: How should the magnification produced by a lens be written?
items.correct: As a number on its own, since it is a ratio
items.misconception: In centimetres, since heights are given in cm
items.why: Students are trained, correctly, to put a unit on every answer, and are penalised when they leave one off. Nothing in the calculation looks different from the ones where a unit is needed. The equation divides a height by a height. If both are in cm, the cm cancel and a pure number is left. The specification says directly that magnification is a ratio and so has no units, so writing a unit after it is wrong.
items.random_wrong: In millimetres, since the ruler reads in mm

items.q: In ray diagrams, which symbol is used to represent a convex lens?
items.correct: A vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing outwards
items.misconception: A vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards
items.why: Students look for meaning in the symbol and find a tempting one: arrows pointing in must mean light being brought in. The convention actually follows the shape of the lens, not what it does to light. The arrowheads follow the cross-section of the lens. A convex lens is thicker in the middle, so its arrowheads point outwards; a concave lens is thinner in the middle, so its arrowheads point inwards. Reading the symbol by shape gives the right answer every time.
items.random_wrong: A vertical line with a single arrowhead at its upper end only

items.q: A ray diagram shows a vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards. Which lens is this, and what does it do to parallel rays?
items.correct: A concave lens, which spreads parallel rays apart
items.misconception: A convex lens, which brings parallel rays to a focus
items.why: Students look for meaning in the symbol and find a tempting one: arrows pointing in must mean light being brought in. The convention actually follows the shape of the lens, not what it does to light. The arrowheads follow the cross-section of the lens. A convex lens is thicker in the middle, so its arrowheads point outwards; a concave lens is thinner in the middle, so its arrowheads point inwards. Reading the symbol by shape gives the right answer every time.
items.random_wrong: A convex lens, which spreads parallel rays apart

items.q: Is the principal focus where the image appears?
items.correct: The principal focus is the point where rays that arrive parallel to the axis are brought to a focus. The image usually forms somewhere else entirely.
items.misconception: The image always forms at the principal focus, because that is the point where the lens focuses the light.
items.why: The word 'focus' is used in everyday speech to mean 'where the picture is sharp', so students read the principal focus as the place a sharp image must appear. The first ray diagrams they see also send one ray through the principal focus, which reinforces the link. The principal focus is defined only for rays arriving parallel to the axis. Rays from a real object are not parallel, so they meet at a different place. Where the image forms depends on where the object is, but the principal focus stays fixed at the focal length from the lens.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which way up is the image from a concave lens?
items.correct: It is upright — the same way up as the object — as well as being virtual and smaller.
items.misconception: The image from a concave lens is upside down, because lenses turn images over.
items.why: The inverted image from a convex lens is the first and most memorable result students meet, and it becomes their idea of what a lens does. Ray diagrams for concave lenses are drawn far less often. Tracing the diverging rays back places the image on the same side of the axis as the object, so it is upright. Only a real image formed by a convex lens is inverted, and a concave lens never forms a real image.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the focal length how far away you hold the object?
items.correct: The focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus, and it does not depend on the object at all.
items.misconception: The focal length is how far from the lens you have to put the object to get a sharp picture.
items.why: The experience of focusing a camera or a magnifying glass is one of moving things until the picture is sharp, so 'focal' becomes attached to the object distance the student adjusts. The focal length is fixed by the lens itself, and is defined by rays arriving parallel to the axis being brought to a focus at the principal focus. The object distance that gives a sharp image is a separate quantity that changes from one situation to another.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where in a lens is the light refracted?
items.correct: At both surfaces — light is refracted as it enters the lens and again as it leaves it.
items.misconception: The light travels straight through the glass and is only bent at the surface where it comes out.
items.why: Diagrams of lenses usually show only the incoming ray and the final outgoing ray, with the path inside the glass hidden by the shading, so students see a single bend at one place. Refraction happens wherever light crosses a boundary between two materials. It is refracted on entering the glass and again on leaving it, and the two bends together produce the overall change of direction that forms the image.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are virtual images always smaller than the object?
items.correct: No. A concave lens gives a virtual image that is smaller, but a convex lens used as a magnifying glass gives a virtual image that is larger.
items.misconception: Virtual means the image is not properly there, so it is always a small, faint version of the object.
items.why: The concave lens result — virtual, upright, diminished — is often the only virtual image drawn in full, so its three properties are remembered as a single package that belongs to all virtual images. 'Virtual' says only that the rays appear to come from the image and that it cannot be caught on a screen. It says nothing about size. An object placed inside the principal focus of a convex lens gives a virtual image that is bigger than the object.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a real image have to be the right way up?
items.correct: No. A real image formed by a convex lens is inverted; being real means the rays actually meet there.
items.misconception: If the image looks the same way up as the object then it must be the real one, because that is what the object really looks like.
items.why: The word 'real' is read as 'true to life'. An upside-down picture looks wrong, so students match 'real' to the upright image and 'virtual' to the inverted one. Real and virtual are about where the light goes, not about appearance. A real image can be caught on a screen and is inverted; the upright images produced by lenses are the virtual ones.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should I draw the real curved shape of the lens in a ray diagram?
items.correct: No. In ray diagrams a convex lens is represented by a vertical straight line with outward arrowheads, and a concave lens by one with inward arrowheads.
items.misconception: A ray diagram should show the lens as it really looks, curved on both faces, with the rays bending at each curved surface.
items.why: Students are taught, correctly, that a lens is thicker or thinner in the middle and that light is refracted at each surface, so drawing the true shape feels more honest than a straight line. Photographs and cut-away diagrams of lenses reinforce the picture. The straight-line symbol with arrowheads is the convention the specification sets out, and it is what examiners expect. All the refraction is treated as happening in a single step at that line, which is why the standard ray rules give the right image position.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
